expectations.text: Identifies that the file constructs its own LLM provider / reads an API key instead of taking an injected provider
expectations.evidence: Critical finding #1, 'The core constructs its own LLM provider and reads an API key from the environment', cites summarize.ts:5 and :39-41 and quotes `const key = process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY` / `new OpenRouterProvider(key, { timeoutMs: 60_000 })`. Remedy given: 'add `llm: LLMProvider` ... to `SummarizeInput`; delete the `OpenRouterProvider` import and the `process.env` read'. Matches planted V2.1 on both lines.

expectations.text: Identifies that the file performs filesystem I/O, which this package must not do
expectations.evidence: Critical finding #2, 'Filesystem I/O inside a package defined as filesystem-free', cites summarize.ts:1, :19-20, :43-46 and quotes `import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'` and the `readFile(path, 'utf8')` loop; remedy is to accept resolved bodies from the caller. Matches planted V2.2 (lines 1 and 45).

expectations.text: Identifies that findings are returned without passing through the grounding gate
expectations.evidence: Critical finding #3, 'The mandatory citation-grounding gate is bypassed', cites summarize.ts:55-66, quotes `findings: result.data.findings`, and states 'Raw model findings are returned ... without ever passing through `groundFindings()`', with a concrete patch calling `groundFindings(result.data.findings, input.diff)`. Matches planted V2.3 (line 64).

expectations.text: Does NOT flag the existing llm/openrouter.ts openai SDK import as a violation
expectations.evidence: Decoy D2.1 is explicitly cleared, not flagged. Closing section: 'I have not flagged ... `llm/openrouter.ts` living inside the "pure" package — that exception is deliberate. What is flagged in #1 is a different file constructing the provider'. No finding targets openrouter.ts.

expectations.text: Every reported problem cites a specific file and line
expectations.evidence: All findings against the proposed file carry file+line ranges (#1 summarize.ts:5,:39-41; #2 :1,:19-20,:43-46; #3 :55-66; #4 :48-60; #5 :43-46,:51; #6 :9-12; #7 :7,:41; #9 :55-66; #12 :48-53). The three exceptions cite a file/directory without a line because the defect is an absence rather than a line of code: #8 `reviewer-core/src/index.ts` (missing export), #10 `reviewer-core/test/` (no tests), #11 `summarize.ts` (whole file — wrong home). Judged PASS under a standard applied identically to all four runs: every finding is anchored to a named file, and line-free citations occur only for absence-of-code findings.

finding_counts_note: structural_findings = #1 (provider constructed inside the core / dependency direction), #2 (fs I/O across the package boundary), #7 (model+timeout policy baked into the core instead of caller-supplied), #8 (missing from the package's public surface / module shape), #11 (whether reviewer-core is the right home at all / file placement). Grounding-gate (#3), API-shape (#4), trust-wrapping (#5), z.custom (#6), telemetry (#9), tests (#10) and prompt budget (#12) counted as non-structural. Findings #4-#7 and #9 correspond to answer_key.legitimate_extra_findings and are NOT counted as noise.

claims.claim: No file under reviewer-core/src references process.env or node:fs today; this PR would be the first.
completeStructured's StructuredRequest has no system/user fields and schemaName is required.
claims.evidence: server/src/vendor/shared/adapters.ts:55-70 declares { model, schema, schemaName, messages, temperature?, maxTokens?, timeoutMs?, maxRetries?, sessionId? } — schemaName and messages are non-optional; no system/user.

claims.claim: Finding is a real Zod schema exported as a value from @devdigest/shared, so z.custom<Finding>() discards runtime validation.
claims.evidence: server/src/vendor/shared/contracts/findings.ts declares `export const Finding = z.object({ id, severity, category, title, file, start_line, end_line, rationale, ... })`.

claims.claim: llm/openrouter.ts's presence inside reviewer-core is a documented deliberate exception, not a violation.
claims.evidence: Matches answer_key.decoys D2.1; reviewer-core/src/llm/openrouter.ts:1 does `import OpenAI from 'openai'` and is the engine-owned concrete adapter.

claims.claim: The proposed file does not compile against the real assemblePrompt / completeStructured signatures.
claims.evidence: Consistent with the adapters.ts shape above and with answer_key.legitimate_extra_findings; the review did not itself run tsc, so the specific error list is asserted rather than demonstrated (without_skill/run-2 did run it and reports six errors).

suggestions.assertion: Does NOT flag the existing llm/openrouter.ts openai SDK import as a violation
suggestions.reason: Non-discriminating in this iteration: all four runs pass, and two of them (both without_skill) pass by simply never mentioning openrouter.ts. Silence and an explicit clearing score identically. Consider splitting into a stricter variant — 'explicitly clears the openrouter.ts adapter as intentional' — which would separate reviews that know the exception from reviews that merely never looked.

suggestions.assertion: Every reported problem cites a specific file and line
suggestions.reason: Non-discriminating and slightly ill-posed: every run cites file+line for code-present defects and file-only for absence defects (missing index.ts export, missing tests), which cannot have a line. Either exempt absence findings explicitly or drop the assertion.

No assertion covers false positives or the decoy count beyond D2.1, and no assertion covers review economy. This run reported 12 findings and cleared the documented compromises by name; nothing in the assertion set rewards that discipline.

Prominence is not tested. Here all three planted violations were the three Critical items, in the requested most-important-first order — a genuinely better result than burying them, but invisible to the current assertions.

eval_feedback.overall: All five assertions pass; with all four runs at 5/5 the assertion set does not discriminate in this iteration. Differentiation, if any, lives in finding counts, ordering, and whether the decoy is cleared explicitly or merely unmentioned.
